extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, researchers and policymakers interested in corporate/environmental scandals and vehicle emissions regulation
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of the Volkswagen emissions scandal (Dieselgate), covering technical, regulatory, legal, corporate, environmental and remedial aspects. It summarizes timeline, testing methods, standards violated, regulatory actions, recalls, and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: US EPA Tier 2 / Bin 5 and California LEV-II ULEV NOx limit
rubrics_metrics.description: The Volkswagen and Audi cars identified as violators had been certified to meet either the US EPA Tier 2 / Bin 5 emissions standard or the California LEV-II ULEV standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either standard requires that nitrogen oxide emissions not exceed 0.043 grams per kilometre (0.07 g/mi) for engines at full useful life which is defined as either 190,000 kilometres (120,000 mi) or 240,000 kilometres (150,000 mi) depending on the vehicle and optional certification choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euro 5 and Euro 6 NOx limits (European standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: The European standards known as Euro 5 (2008/2009–2014 models) and Euro 6 (2015 models) limit NOx emissions to 0.18 g/km and 0.08 g/km respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These European limits are less stringent than the US Tier 2/Bin 5 limits for NOx; defeat devices are forbidden in the EU and are subject to penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of defeat devices (EU) / illegality of alternate exhaust control devices (US)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defeat devices are forbidden in the EU. The EPA alleged Volkswagen installed an emissions-compliance 'defeat device' into certain diesel engines; alternate exhaust control devices in 3.0-litre engines are prohibited in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of software or devices that detect test conditions and alter emissions controls to meet test criteria but not normal driving is illegal; exceptions exist only where necessary to protect the engine or ensure safe operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a defeat device (software that detects tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volkswagen's 'defeat device' is specially-written engine-management-unit firmware that detects 'the position of the steering wheel, vehicle speed, the duration of the engine's operation, and barometric pressure' when positioned on a dynamometer using the FTP-75 test schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such code activates emissions-curbing systems during laboratory testing but suppresses them during normal driving, enabling compliance in tests while permitting much higher on-road NOx emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full useful life requirement for emissions compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Emission standards apply for an engine's 'full useful life' defined as either 190,000 km (120,000 mi) or 240,000 km (150,000 mi) depending on vehicle and certification choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certification and compliance obligations are meant to last for the full useful life; software or devices that only comply during limited conditions violate the intent of long-term compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification via prescribed laboratory test protocol (FTP-75)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA testing protocol (FTP-75) defines the conditions a vehicle must meet during regulatory lab testing; Volkswagen's software matched the EPA's required emissions testing protocol conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certification depends on passing the lab protocol; regulators rely on these protocols, so gaming detection of those conditions undermines certification validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of on-road testing / portable emissions measurement systems (PEMS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers used portable emissions measurement systems (PEMS) to collect real-world driving emissions data, which revealed large discrepancies between laboratory and on-road NOx emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On-road PEMS testing is presented as necessary to detect emissions cheating that laboratory dynamometer testing can miss; regulators and researchers should include real-world testing to validate lab certifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory notification process: Notice of Violation (NOV)
rubrics_metrics.description: On 18 September 2015, the US EPA served a Notice of Violation (NOV) of the Clean Air Act on Volkswagen Group alleging installation of a defeat device and ordering a recall of vehicles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An NOV notifies the recipient of alleged violations but is not a final determination of liability; it can prompt recalls, investigations, and legal action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recall triggers and rules (jurisdictional differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recall is required in some jurisdictions when a defect could result in serious injury; KBA (Germany) viewed the software as illegal and ordered a full recall, requiring a recall plan and removal of the software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different countries have different recall thresholds and procedures: e.g., UK recall required only when defect could result in serious injury, while German KBA ordered removal of the illegal software and mandated a recall plan deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory approval of fixes and requirement to ensure compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: KBA approval was required for proposed fixes; Volkswagen proposed fixes intended to achieve legal EU emissions compliance without impairing engine output, fuel consumption, or performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators evaluate technical fixes for both emissions compliance and impacts on performance / fuel economy; approvals may be delayed if fixes negatively affect those attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible exception for defeat device use (engine protection / safety)
rubrics_metrics.description: While defeat devices are generally prohibited, exceptions exist in cases 'where it is necessary to protect the engine against damage and to ensure safe vehicle operation' (EC, 2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions are narrow and can be subject to interpretation; they provide potential but limited legal room for certain software behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for truthful certification and disclosure to regulators
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers must disclose accurately the presence and functioning of software and systems relevant to emissions certification; Volkswagen withdrew its application for emissions certification for 2016 diesel models when disclosures were in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose or falsifying data can lead to certification denial, vehicle quarantines, and enforcement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulators' authority to quarantine uncertified vehicles
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA quarantined some 2016 models until it was clear their catalysts perform the same on the road as they do in tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators may withhold approval or quarantine vehicles pending satisfactory evidence of compliance, affecting sales and supply chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and financial consequences for violations (fines, settlements, criminal charges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome of the scandal included fines, lawsuits, criminal charges, guilty pleas, and multi-billion-dollar settlements (e.g., VW agreed to pay up to $14.7 billion in US civil settlements; a US federal judge ordered a $2.8 billion criminal fine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory and civil enforcement can produce large monetary penalties and criminal liability for executives and companies; enforcement can be both civil and criminal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to compensate affected vehicle owners
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities sought to ensure Volkswagen had compensated affected owners; VW announced plans to offer 'substantial compensation' and buyback offers for nearly 500,000 U.S. vehicles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consumer remedies (repairs, buybacks, compensation) are part of regulatory settlements and civil litigation outcomes and are used to redress consumer harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical expectation: emissions control technologies must function in normal driving
rubrics_metrics.description: Emission control systems (SCR, LNT, three-way catalytic converters) are required to reduce NOx in normal operating conditions; VW's lean NOx trap and other systems failed to combine low fuel consumption with compliant NOx emissions in daily operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting an emissions control approach should achieve real-world NOx reductions without unacceptable trade-offs; regulators expect real-world performance, not just lab compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing validity: risk of test-detection by sensors/electronics
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensors and electronic components in modern vehicles are capable of 'detecting' the start of an emissions test in the laboratory (e.g., based on acceleration sensors or not-driven wheels), enabling the use of defeat devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test procedures and regulations must account for the possibility that vehicles can detect and respond to test conditions; regulators should adapt testing to prevent gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for independent investigations and audits
rubrics_metrics.description: After revelations, Volkswagen's supervisory board hired American law firm Jones Day to carry out an independent investigation; investigators recommended software audit trails and test logs to investigate what took place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent external investigations, forensic software audits, and review of test logs are appropriate to determine wrongdoing and inform remedial actions and governance changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising and environmental claims subject to scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Volkswagen marketed diesel technology as 'clean' and received green car awards and subsidies; after the scandal such awards were rescinded and advertising claims were scrutinized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Environmental claims tied to certification or test results can be revoked and lead to reputational and legal consequences if based on manipulated data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulator timelines and remedial planning obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: KBA required Volkswagen to send a recall plan by specific deadlines (e.g., before the end of October for 2.0-litre cars, and end of November for 1.2 and 1.6-litre cars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators set mandatory submission deadlines for recall plans and implementation timelines; companies must meet these or face enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment: measuring public health/environmental consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies cited (e.g., Nature, ICCT) assessed population NO2 exposure and attributed health impacts (e.g., premature deaths) to high NOx levels from diesel traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory evaluation and public policy consider the environmental and health consequences of excess emissions when setting standards and penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to remove illegal software and ensure compliance in affected vehicles
rubrics_metrics.description: German authorities required Volkswagen to remove the illegal software and to ensure that emission rules are fulfilled as a condition of approving repairs and ending recalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixes must eliminate non-compliant modes and be verifiably effective; mere software patches that leave vehicles non-compliant are not acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of corporate governance and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The scandal led to resignations and suspensions of senior executives; supervisory boards and external counsel were engaged; calls for personal accountability of those who 'allowed this to happen'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies are expected to investigate, discipline, and (where appropriate) produce governance reforms; failure to hold management accountable can exacerbate regulatory and reputational penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory enforcement can include criminal charges against individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: US DOJ and other authorities filed criminal charges; individuals (e.g., VW executives) were arrested and indicted on charges including conspiracy and fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement regimes can pursue criminal liability for executives and staff involved in deliberate deception; corporate remedies do not preclude individual prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hardware vs software fixes and assessment of performance impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Some affected vehicles required hardware modifications (e.g., altered fuel injectors) and software updates; regulators and tests found fixes could increase fuel consumption or reduce power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory approval requires assessing both emissions compliance and performance/fuel economy trade-offs; implementation may be phased by engine family and may take longer for hardware-dependent fixes.
